text.en: Asha poured water into a glass. "Where does all our water come from?" she asked.

The hydrosphere includes Earth’s water in all its states, including the oceans, rivers, groundwater, ice and water vapour. About 71 percent of the surface is covered by water, but most is salty. The water cycle moves water by evaporation, condensation and precipitation.
Ocean water moves as waves, tides and currents. Tides are regular changes in sea level caused mainly by differences in the Moon’s and Sun’s gravitational effects across Earth. Alignment near new and full moon tends to increase the tidal range. Ocean currents move heat and can affect coastal climate. Currents that bring nutrients toward the surface can also affect marine food webs and fisheries.
The ocean floor has continental shelves, slopes, deep plains and trenches. Fresh water must be saved, as only a small part is usable.

Most of Earth’s water is in the ocean. Only a small share is fresh water, and much of the fresh water is stored in ice or underground.

board.text: Most water is salty; much fresh water is stored

text.en: Evaporation changes liquid water into vapour. Plants also release water vapour through transpiration. Both processes can add moisture to the air.
When moist air cools, some water can condense into droplets. Water can then return as precipitation such as rain or snow. Follow the change in state along the way.
After rain reaches land, runoff can flow to streams or the ocean. Infiltration carries some water into spaces in soil and rock.

board.text: Runoff: over land · infiltration: into land

text.en: Fresh water can be stored in lakes, glaciers or underground for different lengths of time. The water cycle links these stores without moving all water at the same speed.

board.text: Water moves among stores over different timescales

text.en: Oceans are connected. We give names to large regions such as the Pacific and Indian Oceans, but there are no physical walls separating them.
A continental shelf is the gently sloping, underwater extension near a continent’s coast. Its shallow water differs from that over the deeper ocean basin.
At the shelf edge, the continental slope descends toward deeper water. In many places, deposited sediment builds a gentler continental rise near the base of the slope.

board.text: Shelf → slope → rise in many regions

text.en: A deep-ocean plain can be broad and relatively flat because sediment fills low areas. The ocean floor also includes raised features such as mid-ocean ridges.

board.text: Abyssal plain: deep and broadly flat

text.en: A trench is a long, narrow depression. Many very deep trenches occur at plate boundaries where one tectonic plate descends beneath another.

board.text: Trenches often occur at subduction boundaries

text.en: Wind can transfer energy to the water surface and create waves. In many waves, water mostly moves around short paths while the wave pattern carries energy onward.
As a wave enters shallow coastal water, its shape and speed can change. Waves can move sediment along a shore and alter beaches over time.
Tidal range is the difference between high and low tide levels. It varies with the Moon and Sun’s positions and with the shape and depth of the coast.

board.text: Tidal range = high water minus low water

text.en: Near new or full moon, the Sun, Earth and Moon are roughly aligned. Their tidal effects tend to give a larger tidal range, called a spring tide.
Near the first or third quarter moon, the Sun and Moon are roughly at right angles as viewed from Earth. The range is generally smaller then, in a neap tide.
Currents are sustained flows of ocean water. Wind helps drive many surface currents. Differences in density linked to temperature and salinity help drive some deeper flows.

board.text: Wind and density help drive currents

text.en: A warm current can transfer heat toward a cooler region. A cold current can affect nearby coastal temperatures. Land, air and ocean interact in these climate patterns.
When deeper water rises toward the surface in a process called upwelling, nutrients can become available there. These nutrients can support marine food webs.
People use the oceans for food, transport and other resources. A resource can become harder to renew or use when its habitat is damaged or it is taken too quickly.

board.text: Marine resources depend on ecosystem conditions

text.en: Litter and pollution can travel from land into rivers and the sea. Reducing waste at its source can help limit what reaches marine habitats.

board.text: Land and ocean pollution routes are connected

text.en: Keeping waterways clean and using freshwater carefully matter because accessible fresh water is limited. A decision about use should consider quality as well as quantity.

board.text: Freshwater access depends on amount and quality

text.en: Compare an ocean-floor diagram with a water-cycle diagram. In the first, read changes in depth. In the second, follow changes in state or movement between locations.

board.text: Read the feature that the diagram represents

problem.en: A ship crosses from shallow water near a continent to a steep descent and then a broad deep area. Name the three floor features.

text.en: Identify the broad shallow part and the steeper descent.

why.en: These are the continental shelf and continental slope.

text.en: Find the broad, nearly level deep area.

why.en: This shape is characteristic of an abyssal plain.
